title: Naval on Business Specificity, Power Laws, and Why Understanding Beats Memorization
summary: Naval says his real expertise is taking a specific technology business apart and predicting what will work, not abstract wealth advice. He explains power-law outcomes, common founder mistakes, and why understanding, judgment and taste matter more than memorization in the age of AI.

principles.text: Business advice is contextual; real insight comes from dissecting a specific business and entrepreneur, not abstract timeless claims.
principles.quote: business is very very very contextual like you have to look at the particular business and understand what's being done and why it's being done and how it's being done and then you can tear it apart

principles.text: Startup outcomes follow a power law, so you only need to be right a few times, even once, to win big.
principles.quote: number one is going to return more than two through n put together two will return more than three through put together you're operating in a highly leveraged intellectual domain so the outcomes are going to be nonlinear

principles.text: Do the thing you actually want directly instead of using it as a stepping stone to something else.
principles.quote: You're doing A so you can get to B. Just go to B.

principles.text: A founder who loves the product will beat one who is in it for the money.
principles.quote: You're doing this to make money when really the person who's doing this because they love the product is going to beat you.

principles.text: Founder fundamentals fail early: wrong investors, wrong co-founder, wrong vesting, wrong location, or wrong angle.
principles.quote: you're raising money from the wrong people who are in it for the wrong reasons. or your co-founder is not in it for the right reasons or you don't have the right kind of co-founder or your vesting schedule is wrong

principles.text: Memorization is obsolete; understanding, judgment and taste come from solving real problems and finding the commonalities.
principles.quote: Understanding is a thing. Being able to being able Judgment is the thing. Taste is a thing. Um, and understanding, judgment, taste, these come out of having real problems and then solving them
